In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity''' of a [[coherent sheaf]] ''F'' over [[projective space]] <math>\mathbf{P}^n</math> is the smallest integer ''r'' such that it is '''r-regular''', meaning that

:<math>H^i(\mathbf{P}^n, F(r-i))=0</math>

whenever <math>i>0</math>. The regularity of a [[subscheme]] is defined to be the regularity of its sheaf of ideals. The regularity controls when the [[Hilbert function]] of the sheaf becomes a polynomial; more precisely dim <math>H^0(\mathbf{P}^n, F(m))</math> is a polynomial in ''m'' when ''m'' is at least the regularity. The concept of ''r''-regularity  was introduced by {{harvs|txt|author-link=David Mumford|first=David|last=Mumford|year=1966|loc=lecture 14}}, who attributed the following results to  {{harvs|txt|first=Guido| last=Castelnuovo|author-link=Guido Castelnuovo|year=1893}}:
*An ''r''-regular sheaf is ''s''-regular for any <math>s\ge r</math>.
*If a coherent sheaf is ''r''-regular then <math>F(r)</math> is [[generated by its global sections]].

==Graded modules==
A related idea exists in [[commutative algebra]].  Suppose <math>R= k[x_0,\dots,x_n]</math> is a [[polynomial ring]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''k'' and ''M'' is a [[Finitely-generated module|finitely generated]] [[Graded algebra#Graded module|graded ''R''-module]].  Suppose ''M'' has a [[Resolution (algebra)#Graded modules and algebras|minimal graded free resolution]]
:<math>\cdots\rightarrow F_j \rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow F_0\rightarrow M\rightarrow 0</math>
and let <math>b_j</math> be the maximum of the degrees of the generators of <math>F_j</math>.  If ''r'' is an integer such that <math>b_j - j \le r</math> for all ''j'', then ''M'' is said to be ''r''-regular.  The regularity of ''M'' is the smallest such ''r''.

These two notions of regularity coincide when ''F'' is a coherent sheaf such that <math>\operatorname{Ass}(F)</math> contains no closed points.  Then the graded module 
:<math>M=\bigoplus_{d \in \Z} H^0(\mathbf{P}^n,F(d))</math> 
is finitely generated and has the same regularity as ''F''.
